title: Moles from mass and molar mass
body: n = \frac{m}{M}
ced_evidence: 1.1.A EQN: n = m/M

title: Avogadro's number
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.2 Avogadro's number (NA = 6.022 × 10^23 mol−1)

title: amu per particle equals grams per mole
body: The average mass in amu of one particle or formula unit of a substance is numerically equal to the molar mass of that substance in grams.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.3 average mass in amu of one particle ... numerically equal to the molar mass of that substance in grams

title: Mass spectrum of a single element
body: A graph of relative abundance versus mass for the isotopes of one element.

items.label: Peak position (x-axis)
items.meaning: Mass of an isotope, which identifies the isotope

items.label: Peak height (y-axis)
items.meaning: Relative abundance of that isotope in nature

caution: Isotopes of one element differ in mass because they have different numbers of neutrons, not different numbers of protons or electrons. Read the y-axis scale carefully when estimating abundances.
ced_evidence: 1.2.A.1 identity of the isotopes of that element and the relative abundance of each isotope in nature

title: Average atomic mass from isotope data
body: \text{average atomic mass} = \sum_i \left(f_i \times m_i\right)
caution: Here f_i is the fractional abundance (percent divided by 100) of isotope i and m_i is its mass.
ced_evidence: 1.2.A.2 weighted average of the isotopic masses using the mass of each isotope and its relative abundance

title: Formula unit
body: A formula unit describes the fixed proportions in which the atoms or ions of a pure substance that is not made of individual molecules are held together.
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.1 atoms or ions held together in fixed proportions as described by a formula unit

title: Law of definite proportions
body: The ratio of the masses of the constituent elements in any pure sample of a compound is always the same.
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.2 law of definite proportions

title: Empirical formula
body: The empirical formula is the chemical formula that lists the lowest whole-number ratio of atoms of the elements in a compound.
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.3 lowest whole number ratio of atoms of the elements in a compound is the empirical formula

title: Pure substance
body: A pure substance contains atoms, molecules, or formula units of a single type.
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.1 Pure substances contain atoms, molecules, or formula units of a single type

title: Mixture
body: A mixture contains atoms, molecules, or formula units of two or more types whose relative proportions can vary.
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.1 Mixtures contain atoms, molecules, or formula units of two or more types, whose relative proportions can vary

title: Uses of elemental analysis
body: Elemental analysis can be used to determine the relative numbers of atoms in a substance and to determine its purity.
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.2 Elemental analysis can be used to determine the relative numbers of atoms in a substance and to determine its purity

title: Coulomb's law
body: F_{\text{coulombic}} \propto \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.2 EQN: Fcoulombic ∝ q1q2/r^2

title: Atom composition
body: An atom is composed of negatively charged electrons and a positively charged nucleus made of protons and neutrons.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.1 negatively charged electrons and a positively charged nucleus that is made of protons and neutrons

title: Shells and subshells
body: Electrons in atoms and ions are described as occupying shells (energy levels) and subshells (sublevels), as given by the ground-state electron configuration.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.3 “shells (energy levels)” and “subshells (sublevels)”

title: Core electrons
body: Core electrons are the inner electrons of an atom or ion.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.3 Inner electrons are called core electrons

title: Valence electrons
body: Valence electrons are the outer electrons of an atom or ion.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.3 outer electrons are called valence electrons

title: Aufbau subshell filling order
body: Order in which subshells are filled to write the ground-state electron configuration of an atom.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A Represent the ground-state electron configuration ... using the Aufbau principle

hooks.hook_text: Diagonal rule: write the subshells in rows by shell number, then follow diagonal arrows from upper right to lower left.
hooks.when_to_use: Use it to recall the order of subshell filling when writing a ground-state configuration.

title: Ionization energy
body: Ionization energy is the relative energy required to remove an electron from a subshell of an atom or ion, estimated qualitatively with Coulomb's law from the electron's distance from the nucleus and the effective nuclear charge.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.4 relative energy required to remove an electron ... (ionization energy)

title: Effective (shielded) nuclear charge
body: Effective nuclear charge is the net positive nuclear charge an electron experiences after other electrons shield it from the nucleus.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.4 the effective (shield) charge of the nucleus; 1.7.A.2 shielding and effective nuclear charge

title: Photoelectron spectrum (PES)
body: A plot of peaks, one per subshell, used to relate the spectrum to electron configuration and electron-nucleus interactions.

items.label: Peak position
items.meaning: Energy required to remove an electron from the corresponding subshell

items.label: Relative peak height
items.meaning: Ideally proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell

ced_evidence: 1.6.A.1 position of each peak ... related to the energy required to remove an electron ... relative height ... proportional to the number of electrons

title: Periodic properties explained by electronic structure
body: The atomic properties whose periodic trends the CED requires students to predict and explain.
ced_evidence: 1.7.A.2 These properties include: i. Ionization energy ii. Atomic and ionic radii iii. Electron affinity iv. Electronegativity

title: Tools for explaining periodic trends
body: Trends are predicted from an element's position on the periodic table and explained qualitatively with these four ideas.

items.label: Coulomb's law
items.meaning: Attraction depends on charges and distance

items.label: Shell model
items.meaning: Electrons occupy shells at different distances from the nucleus

items.label: Shielding
items.meaning: Other electrons reduce the attraction an electron feels

items.label: Effective nuclear charge
items.meaning: Net nuclear charge experienced by an electron

ced_evidence: 1.7.A.2 qualitatively understood using Coulomb's law, the shell model, and the concepts of shielding and effective nuclear charge

title: Periodic table organization and prediction
body: The periodic table is organized by recurring properties explained by ground-state electron configurations and filled or partially filled shells and subshells, so periodicity can be used to estimate property values when data are absent.
ced_evidence: 1.7.A.1 patterns of recurring properties; 1.7.A.3 predict/estimate values of properties in the absence of data

title: Bond likelihood from valence electrons and nuclei
body: Whether two elements will form a chemical bond is determined by the interactions between their valence electrons and nuclei.
ced_evidence: 1.8.A.1 determined by the interactions between the valence electrons and nuclei of elements

title: Same column, analogous compounds
body: Elements in the same column of the periodic table tend to form analogous compounds.
ced_evidence: 1.8.A.2 Elements in the same column of the periodic table tend to form analogous compounds

title: Typical ionic charge from periodic table position
body: The typical charge of an atom in an ionic compound is governed by its number of valence electrons and predicted from its location on the periodic table.
ced_evidence: 1.8.A.3 Typical charges of atoms in ionic compounds are governed by the number of valence electrons
